summary.text: Obsidian is a natural volcanic glass that forms when lava from a volcano cools so fast that very few crystals can grow.
Its lava is high in silica and very thick, which stops atoms from moving into place to start crystals, so together with fast cooling it sets as glass.
Being hard, brittle and without crystal structure, it breaks with very sharp edges, which is why Stone Age people shaped it into blades and arrowheads.

facts.label: Main ingredient
facts.value: Silicon dioxide, usually 70% by weight or more

facts.label: Mineral status
facts.value: Not a true mineral; sometimes called a mineraloid

facts.label: Black color
facts.value: Most black obsidian holds tiny magnetite inclusions

items.prompt: Two rocks came from the same silica-rich lava. One is full of crystals; the other is smooth, shiny glass. What most likely happened to the glassy one?

options.label: It held far more iron than the other
Its lava cooled very quickly
It cooled slowly deep underground
It was buried longer under pressure

items.explain: Obsidian forms when lava cools rapidly, leaving almost no time for crystals to grow, so it sets as glass.

items.prompt: A Stone Age toolmaker chooses obsidian for an arrowhead. What property of the stone matters most?

options.label: It is soft enough to carve with bone
It is heavy enough to fly straight
It breaks into very sharp edges
It bends slightly without snapping

items.explain: Obsidian is hard, brittle and has no crystal structure, so it fractures with very sharp edges that can be knapped into blades and points.

items.prompt: Obsidian is usually dark, much like basalt. What is its chemistry actually like?

options.label: Mostly silicon dioxide, like granite
Mostly iron and magnesium, like basalt
Mostly carbon, like coal
Mostly calcium carbonate, like chalk

items.explain: Despite its dark look, obsidian is extremely felsic: usually 70% or more silicon dioxide, similar in makeup to granite and rhyolite.

items.prompt: Collectors hunting for very ancient obsidian, older than the Miocene, find almost none. Why?

options.label: Ancient volcanoes never erupted such lava
Early toolmakers used up the old supply
Wind and rain wore all of it away
Over time the glass turns into tiny crystals

items.explain: Obsidian is metastable at the surface: over time the glass devitrifies into fine-grained mineral crystals, so old obsidian is rare.

items.prompt: A chunk of obsidian lies in damp ground, soaked by groundwater, for a very long time. What happens to it?

options.label: Nothing, since glass is never touched by water
It slowly takes up water and alters into perlite
It dissolves away completely, like salt
It becomes clearer and more glassy

items.explain: Fresh obsidian holds under 1% water, but groundwater gradually hydrates it into perlite, and water speeds up its transformation.

items.prompt: Why don't geologists count obsidian as a true mineral?

options.label: It forms at the surface, not underground
It is too soft to be scratched
It is not crystalline and its makeup varies
It is produced partly by living things

items.explain: As a glass, obsidian is not crystalline, and its composition is too variable for it to be classed as a mineral.
